blocks.text: On the animal's lung Hasselquist writes thus, p. 348: "The lung is single, below the diaphragm, occupying the left hypochondrium; very large, very thin, made up of a few blood vessels and very many air vesicles, which are very distinct and wide; it ends below in 5 or 6 appendages, which are cylindrical, membranous, tubular and unequal, to each of which an air bladder is attached."

Again Hasselquist, p. 349: "The tongue is triangular at the tip, thinned, rough; then muscular, strong, tubular, narrower at the base, very long, with a tubular longitudinal small bone in the middle, which is continued from the hyoid bone."

J. E. FABER sought to prove that Bochart erred in this explanation of the name حربا [ḥrbā] in his Dissertation de Animalibus, quorum mentio fit Zeph. II, 14. (appended by C. F. CRAMER to the book entitled Scythische Denkmäler in Palaestina). After reviewing Bochart's opinion on the word حربا [ḥrbā], he continues thus (p. 305 of the book cited): "But Bochart is quite mistaken. For the name of the spear is rather far from the root, and was derived from it by another route. Rather, [the chameleon] is named from חרב, whose proper force and meaning among the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Syrians lies in drying up, like יבש; for this reason it is said of the drying up of waters, Ies. XIX, 5. LI, 10., and is found joined with יבש, to be dried up. For the chameleon delights in the sun and is, as it were, dried up by its heat." So Faber, who is so far from having corrected Bochart that he has rather himself put forward plain falsehoods. For to the name حِرْباء [ḥirbāʾ], used only in the Arabic dialect, he attributes the notion of drying up, which is entirely foreign to the Arabic verb حَرِبَ [ḥariba]. Next, anyone will feel for himself how unsuitably the chameleon would be thought to be named from drying up because it loves sunny places. Nor is it any more satisfactory that the same Faber holds the Hebrew חרב in Zephan. II, 14. to be the name of the chameleon. He did not consider the usage of the Hebrew language, which consistently employs this word now to denote desolation, now dryness. And there appears no need to reject the notion of desolation in the passage of Zephaniah. How we think that passage should be interpreted we have set out above at book 3, ch. 8, note 7, p. 115.

ويتلون الوانا بحر الشمس وهي الظل اخضر [wa-yatalawwan alwānan bi-ḥarr al-shams wa-hiya al-ẓill akhḍar] it changes colour in the heat of the sun, and is now black, now green. So Nahhas the grammarian on verse 29 of the poem of Kaab son of Zuhair, p. 24 of Lette's edition. Moreover, on the change of colour in the chameleon, worth reading are Hasselquist, p. 350 of the Travels in the German translation, and a certain learned man skilled in natural history, on Belon's Travels, translated by the most celebrated Paulus in the Sylloge Itinerariorum Orientalium (Sammlung der merkwürdigsten Reisen in den Orient) vol. 2, p. 259. 260.

In the Alexandrian version of the passage of Zephaniah, χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes] corresponds to the Hebrew קאת, while κορακα [koraka] corresponds to חרב. But Faber, to add strength and weight to his opinion that חרב means the chameleon, would have the order of those two words disturbed in the manuscripts of the Alexandrian version, so that in place of χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes] κορακες [korakes] should be restored, and in place of κορακες [korakes] χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes]. Since this has been devised in favour of a rather flimsy opinion and rests on no authority, we think it needs no refutation.
